days.review: The intuitive revision habit is *blocking*: all of topic A, then B, then C. It feels smooth and you seem to improve fast within a block. *Interleaving* mixes them — A, C, B, A… Like kicks to a pad held at changing distances, mixed practice is harder but trains adjustment that repetition never does. Today you contrast both on your own material.

task.do: Pick 2 related topics/problem types from your course. Spend 4 minutes blocked on A only, then 4 minutes alternating A↔B every 1–2 minutes (questions, prompts, or recall cues you create). Note which felt smoother and which forced more decisions.
task.capture: Topics A/B, what you practiced in each half, and which required more "which approach?" decisions.

check.q: Which half of today's practice trained exam-like choosing, and what about it forced those decisions?
check.rubric: correct: Interleaved half — had to keep deciding which approach applied; blocked allows autopilot. mostly_correct: Prefers mixing without naming choice skill. incorrect: Blocked half trained choosing better; mixing never affects decisions.
check.exemplar: The interleaved half trained exam-like choosing because I had to keep deciding which approach applied. The blocked half let me run on autopilot within one method.

check.q: Blocked practice felt smoother. What should you conclude about that feeling versus revision quality?
check.rubric: correct: Smoothness often means less decision training — not automatically better revision. mostly_correct: Suspicious of ease vaguely. incorrect: Smoothness proves blocking always superior; difficulty always means wrong method.
check.exemplar: Feeling smoother usually means less decision training, not better revision. Interleaving's messiness is where the transferable choice skill is built.

check.q: What detail in your capture best shows you actually interleaved rather than finished one block then the other?
check.rubric: correct: Rotated A and B before either felt done. mostly_correct: Mentions both topics vaguely. incorrect: Finished all of A before B; only reviewed A; watched solutions only.
check.exemplar: I rotated A and B before either felt finished. Completing all of A before touching B would have been blocking, not interleaving.

days.review: When you block, you already know which method every problem needs. When you interleave, you must first *decide which approach a problem calls for* — exactly what exams and real life test. Mixing also helps memory, test performance, unfamiliar variants, and naturally spaces practice. Today you build a mini set that forces that choice.

task.do: From your notes/problem sets, gather 6 short items that could be confused (3 from type A, 3 from type B). Shuffle them so types are mixed. Solve or answer from memory in shuffled order — about 8–10 minutes. Mark each: right approach chosen? yes/no.
task.capture: The shuffled order (A/B labels), and yes/no for approach choice on each.

check.q: If you missed an item because you used the previous item's method on autopilot, what skill failed?
check.rubric: correct: Selecting which approach the item called for. mostly_correct: Says concentration vaguely. incorrect: Neatness, reading speed only, or page-number memory.
check.exemplar: The skill that failed was selecting which approach the item called for. Autopilot from the previous item is exactly what interleaving is meant to disrupt.

check.q: Looking at your yes/no marks, where should tomorrow's mix focus, and why?
check.rubric: correct: On pairs you mis-classified — highest payoff discrimination practice. mostly_correct: Practice more vaguely. incorrect: Only types already perfect; unrelated subjects; passive solution rereads.
check.exemplar: Tomorrow's mix should focus on the pairs I marked no — mis-chosen approaches show where discrimination practice pays off most.

check.q: Why did shuffling matter for this task compared with AAA then BBB?
check.rubric: correct: Shuffling removes the giveaway that "we are in type A now" so you must choose. mostly_correct: Says mixing helps vaguely. incorrect: Order never matters; blocking forces choice equally.
check.exemplar: Shuffling hid the type label so I had to choose the approach. AAA then BBB advertises the method and removes that decision.

days.review: Interleaving is a *revision* tool. You need a foundational understanding of each topic before mixing, or you are just confused. If you cannot yet do a simple blocked example of A or B, mix practice will thrash. Today you gate interleaving behind a quick readiness check on your own material.

task.do: List 3 candidate topics to interleave. For each, try one easy closed-book example. Label Ready (can do basics) or Not yet (still encoding). Build a mix only from Ready topics; schedule encoding for Not-yet — about 8 minutes.
task.capture: The three labels and the mix set you are allowed to use (Ready only).

check.q: If one topic failed its easy example, what is the correct move regarding your mix — and why?
check.rubric: correct: Keep it out until basics exist; mix Ready only — early interleaving thrash/confusion. mostly_correct: Delay vaguely. incorrect: Force into mix to catch up; drop all interleaving forever.
check.exemplar: I keep that topic out of the mix until basics exist and only interleave Ready topics. Mixing without foundations produces confusion, not discrimination skill.

check.q: If all three were Ready, what is the best next step from today's gate check?
check.rubric: correct: Build a mixed set from those related Ready topics. mostly_correct: Practice them somehow. incorrect: Wait until finals; block another month with no mix; interleave with unrelated hobby topics.
check.exemplar: Next I build a mixed set from those related Ready topics. The readiness gate exists so I can interleave now — not wait until finals.

check.q: A classmate mixes brand-new lecture topics nightly and feels lost. What is the diagnosis?
check.rubric: correct: Interleaving before foundations — revise after basics, do not thrash. mostly_correct: Too early vaguely. incorrect: Needs more unrelated subjects; confusion always means it is working; never use active recall.
check.exemplar: They are interleaving before foundations. Interleaving is a revision tool — mixing brand-new topics creates thrash, not useful difficulty.

days.review: Interleave topics or problem types that could genuinely be confused or combined — not random unrelated subjects. The value is learning to *tell them apart* and choose between them. Mixing chemistry with unrelated history may space time, but it misses discrimination training.

task.do: From your syllabus, pick two pairs: (1) Related — easy to confuse/combine, (2) Unrelated — little overlap. Create a 6-item mix for the Related pair only and run it. Write one sentence on what distinction the mix forced — about 8 minutes.
task.capture: Related pair, Unrelated pair (not practiced), and the distinction your Related mix trained.

check.q: Why did today's task tell you not to practice the Unrelated pair?
check.rubric: correct: Interleaving payoff is discrimination among confusable/combinable types. mostly_correct: Related is better vaguely. incorrect: Unrelated mixes illegal; only identical items; related topics should never mix.
check.exemplar: The payoff is learning to tell confusable or combinable types apart and choose between them. An unrelated mix may space time but misses that discrimination training.

check.q: If your Related mix still felt too easy to tell apart, how should you upgrade the pair?
check.rubric: correct: Choose closer cousins / types you actually mix up on exams. mostly_correct: Make it harder vaguely. incorrect: Switch to unrelated; pure blocking forever; remove decision points.
check.exemplar: I should pick closer cousins or problem types I actually confuse on exams. If discrimination is trivial, the mix is not training the choice skill.

check.q: Give an example from your course of a strong interleaving pair versus a weak one, using today's relatedness rule.
check.rubric: correct: Strong = confusable Ready procedures/types; weak = unrelated courses, identical repeats, or unencoded topics. mostly_correct: Names a pair without contrast. incorrect: Prefers unrelated or unencoded mixes.
check.exemplar: A strong pair is two procedures I often apply to the wrong problem type. A weak pair is a maths drill mixed with unrelated vocabulary from another course.

days.review: Do not finish a topic to completion before rotating. Switch while there is still a little struggle — the switching is the point. Completing every A item "for closure" recreates blocking. Today you practice leaving a thread unfinished on purpose.

task.do: Set a timer for 8 minutes with topics A and B (Ready + related). Work A for ~2 minutes, switch to B at mid-struggle, back to A, back to B. Do not "finish the set" of either. Stop mid-item if the timer says switch.
task.capture: When you switched (what you left unfinished) and how the mid-struggle switches felt.

check.q: If you wanted to finish A's worksheet before touching B, what rule were you about to break — and why does that rule exist?
check.rubric: correct: Switch before you're done — rotation matters more than closure; finishing recreates blocking. mostly_correct: Mentions switching vaguely. incorrect: Always complete blocks for interleaving; only switch when easy.
check.exemplar: I was about to break "switch before you're done." Finishing A for closure recreates blocking; the switching itself is the training.

check.q: What in your capture best shows you followed the rule, and what pattern would show you broke it?
check.rubric: correct: Left items unfinished when switching vs completing all of A then all of B. mostly_correct: Mentions switching without unfinished evidence. incorrect: Only easier topic; avoided struggle by quitting.
check.exemplar: Leaving items unfinished when I switched shows rule-following. Completing all of A, then all of B, would show I broke it.

check.q: Mid-switch frustration spiked. How should you read that feeling during interleaved revision?
check.rubric: correct: Expected desirable difficulty — keep structured switches. mostly_correct: Hard is okay vaguely. incorrect: Proof to return to pure blocking; stop revision; Ready topics were a mistake.
check.exemplar: That frustration is expected desirable difficulty. I should keep structured switches rather than treat discomfort as a stop sign or a reason to return to blocking.

days.review: Like other effective methods, interleaving feels harder and messier than blocking. That discomfort is desirable difficulty doing its job — not proof the method failed. Today you track performance and feeling separately so ease does not hijack your revision choices.

task.do: Run a 6–8 item interleaved set on related Ready material. After each item, jot F (felt easy/hard) and P (process correct: yes/no). Compare whether "felt hard" lined up with "process wrong" — about 8 minutes.
task.capture: Your F/P marks and one sentence on whether hard feelings matched actual errors.

check.q: If several items felt hard but your process was correct, how should you interpret that?
check.rubric: correct: Desirable difficulty — hard feelings ≠ failure of interleaving. mostly_correct: Hard can be okay vaguely. incorrect: Hard feelings always mean stop mixing; only do easy problems.
check.exemplar: Hard feelings with correct process are desirable difficulty. Feeling hard does not mean interleaving failed.

check.q: You nearly switched back to blocking because the session felt messy. What is the better move?
check.rubric: correct: Keep mixing related Ready items; judge by approach accuracy over comfort. mostly_correct: Persist vaguely. incorrect: Abandon when mood dips; only reread examples; mix unrelated for novelty.
check.exemplar: I should keep mixing related Ready items and judge by approach accuracy, not comfort. Messy feel is expected — comfort would recreate blocking.

check.q: Which metric from today's F/P log should drive adjustments, and which should not?
check.rubric: correct: Wrong approach choices (P=no) drive adjustments; F=hard alone should not. mostly_correct: Mentions accuracy vaguely. incorrect: Only pleasant feelings; handwriting; similarity to yesterday's block.
check.exemplar: I should adjust based on wrong approach choices (P = no), not merely on F = hard. Ease ratings are not the training target.

days.review: Once you have encoded a few related topics, build mixed review sets: alternate problem types, shuffle subjects within a session, and mix the kinds of questions you ask yourself. Prepare the set *before* you start so you do not drift back into blocks mid-session.

task.do: Create a 9-item mixed review set from your own materials (3 topics or problem types, Ready + related). Write prompts/problem numbers on a single shuffled list. Complete the set without re-sorting by type — about 9–10 minutes.
task.capture: Paste the shuffled list (short labels) and score approach choice + answer quality briefly.

check.q: If halfway through you regrouped all type-2 items together "to go faster," what did that do to the practice?
check.rubric: correct: Collapsed back toward blocking and removed choice practice. mostly_correct: Hurt interleaving vaguely. incorrect: Improved interleaving; required by the method.
check.exemplar: Regrouping by type collapsed the set back toward blocking and removed the approach-choice practice. I needed to keep the shuffled order.

check.q: What features of your pre-built list best match how interleaving should be used in a session?
check.rubric: correct: Shuffled related types and varied question kinds on one sheet prepared in advance. mostly_correct: Mentions a mix vaguely. incorrect: Separated A then B then C blocks; unencoded new lectures; single stem only.
check.exemplar: My list shuffled related types and varied question kinds on one sheet before I started. Separated blocks labeled A then B then C would not match.

check.q: If two of your three topics were unrelated to the third, how should you fix the set?
check.rubric: correct: Rebuild so every type could be confused or combined with the others. mostly_correct: Change topics vaguely. incorrect: Add more unrelated courses; remove all variety.
check.exemplar: I should rebuild so every type could be confused or combined with the others. Relatedness among mixed items preserves discrimination value.

days.review: Interleaving pairs best with active recall at higher-order levels — not recognition glances in a mixed order. Mixing weak review still yields weak learning. Today every interleaved item must be produced or solved before you check, with at least one compare/choose/explain prompt.

task.do: Run a short interleaved set (6 items, related Ready topics). For each: closed production/solution first; include at least two higher-order prompts (compare, choose approach, explain why not the other method). Check only after each attempt — about 8–10 minutes.
task.capture: List items with type tags, note which were higher-order, and where approach choice failed.

check.q: If you interleaved but peeked at solutions early, what broke — and why can't mixing fix that alone?
check.rubric: correct: Active recall broke; mixing cannot fix recognition-first checking. mostly_correct: Peeking bad vaguely. incorrect: Peeking required for interleaving; only the timer broke.
check.exemplar: Active recall broke. Interleaving amplifies good retrieval — it cannot fix recognition-first peeking.

check.q: Which item in your set best combined interleaving with higher-order thinking? Describe the prompt.
check.rubric: correct: Compare/choose/why-not-the-other on a shuffled confusable pair. mostly_correct: Names a hard item without higher-order feature. incorrect: Recognize highlighted definition; reread summary; copy worked example.
check.exemplar: My best item asked why this method instead of the other on a shuffled confusable pair. That hits both mixing and higher-order choice.

check.q: Where approach choice failed on a higher-order item, what is the best follow-up for future mixes?
check.rubric: correct: Keep that pair in future mixes with which-method/why prompts. mostly_correct: Practice it again vaguely. incorrect: Avoid higher-order prompts; only block forever; drop active recall.
check.exemplar: I should keep that pair in future mixes and re-ask which method and why. Failed discriminations are exactly what to re-interleave.

days.review: Run a complete mini revision: Ready related topics only, pre-shuffled set, switches before closure, expect messiness, retrieve first, include approach-choice questions. This is how interleaving should look in a real study block for your course.

task.do: Prepare and complete a 10–12 minute interleaved session on 2–3 related Ready topics from your exam list: shuffled items, forced switches every ~2 minutes, no peeking first, end with a 1-minute note on which discriminations are still shaky.
task.capture: Session plan (topics + shuffle), shaky discriminations, and one adjustment for next time.

check.q: Which feature of the session you just ran is non-negotiable for real interleaving?
check.rubric: correct: Mixing related Ready material so approach choice stays in play. mostly_correct: Mentions mixing without Ready/related. incorrect: Finish every topic to 100% before switching; only unrelated subjects; must feel smoother than blocking.
check.exemplar: Mixing related Ready material so I still had to choose approaches was non-negotiable. Finishing each topic to completion before switching would have broken it.

check.q: Your shaky-discrimination note lists a pair. How should you design the next session around it?
check.rubric: correct: Heavier mix of that pair with which/why prompts. mostly_correct: Practice the pair vaguely. incorrect: Avoid the pair; long blocks without mixing; recognition highlights.
check.exemplar: Next session should mix that pair more heavily with "which method / why" prompts — not avoid it or bury it in pure blocking.

check.q: The session felt worse than yesterday's blocked review. What does this subject predict about that feeling versus exam-relevant training?
check.rubric: correct: Worse feel can still mean better exam-relevant choice training (desirable difficulty). mostly_correct: Hard can be good vaguely. incorrect: Felt bad means done wrong; blocking always predicts higher scores; feelings are only metric.
check.exemplar: This subject predicts that a worse feel can still mean better exam-relevant training. Desirable difficulty trains the choice skill exams use even when blocking felt nicer.

days.review: Checkpoint with fresh related topics: readiness gate, related-only mix, switch before done, tolerate worse feel, retrieve before checking, and judge approach choice. New scenarios — same hard moves.

task.do: Pick two related Ready topics not used yesterday. Build a 6-item shuffle; mid-struggle switches; mark approach choice yes/no; write one "why not the other method?" answer from memory for a miss.
task.capture: Shuffle labels, yes/no marks, and the why-not-the-other explanation.

check.q: You switched topics while still struggling. Which rule did that practice, and why leave work unfinished on purpose?
check.rubric: correct: Switch before you're done — switching is the point; unfinished struggle preserves interleaving. mostly_correct: Mentions switching vaguely. incorrect: Always finish blocks; mix only unrelated; avoid struggle.
check.exemplar: That practiced "switch before you're done." Leaving unfinished struggle on purpose keeps the rotation — finishing for closure would recreate blocking.

check.q: A miss happened because you treated item 4 like item 3's type. What is the best fix in future sets?
check.rubric: correct: More interleaved reps that hide the type label until you choose. mostly_correct: Be more careful vaguely. incorrect: Longer blocked drills only; stop checking approach; recognition-only reviews.
check.exemplar: I need more interleaved reps that hide the type until I choose. Autopilot from the previous item is exactly what interleaving disrupts — longer blocked drills would reinforce it.

check.q: If your why-not-the-other explanation was vague, what should you train next inside mixed sets?
check.rubric: correct: Conditional discrimination — when/why each approach wins. mostly_correct: Better explanations vaguely. incorrect: Only memorize definitions in order; avoid explanations; block until explanations feel unnecessary.
check.exemplar: I should train conditional discrimination inside mixed sets — when and why each approach wins. Vague why-not answers mean that choice knowledge is still weak.
